answer: Agents can require each participant to lock a scarce, slashable stake before its votes count, then randomly sample participants for repeated, costly work and slash deposits when identities coordinate to submit the same invalid result. Splitting one account into a hundred does not multiply influence: each identity needs its own capital, and detection risks losing it. The ocean of possible names narrows to funded identities; a prism of independent checks helps expose copied behavior, while a comet of new accounts still has to pay the entry cost.
